headline: Oklahoma SB 1 would bar gun license denials for cannabis patients
dek: Oklahoma Senate leader Julie Daniels filed SB 1 for 2027 to bar handgun license denials based only on an applicant's medical marijuana patient license.
key_points: Senate Bill 1, filed by Senate Majority Floor Leader Julie Daniels for the session that starts on 1 February 2027, amends the Oklahoma Self-Defense Act.
The bill says an applicant cannot be found ineligible, and the Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation cannot deny a license, solely because the person holds a medical marijuana patient license.
It also exempts licensed patients from a preclusion tied to pending drug charges, and makes it unlawful to carry a gun while impaired by medical marijuana.
A near-identical bill, SB 39, passed the Senate 45-0 in 2025 but stalled in the House; SB 1 would take effect on 1 November 2027.
body: Oklahoma's Senate Majority Floor Leader, Republican Julie Daniels, has filed a bill for the 2027 session that would stop the state from refusing a handgun license to someone just because they are a registered medical marijuana patient. Senate Bill 1, filed last week, amends the Oklahoma Self-Defense Act, the law that governs concealed and open carry licenses issued by the Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation (OSBI).

The bill matters in a state with one of the largest medical cannabis programs in the country. The Oklahoma Medical Marijuana Authority counted more than 302,000 active standard patient licenses as of 2 November 2026, according to The Marijuana Herald. Filed as SB 1, it sits first in the Senate's numbering for the new session.

The introduced text makes three changes. First, in the list of conditions that automatically bar someone from a handgun license, it adds a sentence saying an applicant shall not be considered ineligible solely because they lawfully hold a medical marijuana patient license. A separate new paragraph says nothing in the law allows the OSBI to deny an otherwise qualified applicant on that basis alone.

Second, it changes one of the temporary preclusions. Under current law, a pending charge or similar matter involving illegal drug use or possession can block a license until the case is resolved. SB 1 carves out applicants and licensees who legally hold a medical marijuana patient license.

Third, it tightens the rule on carrying while impaired. The existing law makes it unlawful to carry or use a shotgun, rifle or pistol while under the influence of alcohol, hallucinogens or unlawful drugs, or of a prescribed drug whose effects cause abnormal behavior. SB 1 adds medical marijuana obtained under a patient license to that last category: carrying is unlawful when its effects or aftereffects impair mental, emotional or physical processes enough to cause abnormal behavior. Penalties stay as they are, including a six-month license suspension and a $50 administrative fine for a licensed holder found in violation.
Other disqualifications are untouched, including felony convictions and outstanding warrants. The bill would take effect on 1 November 2027 if lawmakers pass it and the governor signs it.
> SB 1 does not expand gun rights. It removes one reason the state can give for a no, and pairs that with a clearer impairment rule.

Daniels has tried this before. Her 2025 bill, SB 39, passed the Oklahoma Senate unanimously, 45-0, but never received final approval in the House, The Marijuana Herald reported. Oklahoma law already bars state and local agencies from restricting gun ownership or related licenses only because someone is a patient; SB 1 writes that protection directly into the handgun licensing statute, which is where denials are decided.
On our reading, filing it as SB 1, with the majority floor leader as author and months before the session, gives the bill the earliest possible start and more time to reach the House than SB 39 had.

A state law cannot change federal firearms rules, and the Herald's reading of the bill notes that disqualifications under federal law remain in place. The federal government's April order moved state-licensed medical marijuana activity to Schedule III, but SB 1 does not address how federal gun law treats patients and does not try to. In practice the bill governs the state handgun license that the OSBI issues, not any federal question.
## Where it fits in Oklahoma's cannabis year

SB 1 arrives as Oklahoma's cannabis politics shift. As we reported on 12 November, the Oklahoma Supreme Court struck down new limits on citizen petitions, reopening a path for a legalization measure. And on 15 November we reported that Oklahoma officials warned North Carolina's cannabis advisory council to keep its licensing tight, drawing on Oklahoma's experience with a market that grew faster than its regulators could police.

Oklahoma voters approved medical marijuana through State Question 788 in 2018, and the program's size gives SB 1 a large constituency. The 2025 Senate vote showed no opposition in that chamber. The House is where the bill will be decided.

Monday 1 February 2027: Oklahoma's legislative session opens and SB 1 can be heard. Watch for its committee assignment in the Senate and, if it passes, how quickly the House takes it up, given that SB 39 stalled there. If enacted, the law would take effect on Monday 1 November 2027.
